title: differentiate sums of inverse trigonometric functions whose chain factors cancel or add.
stem: For x > 0, let f(x) = tan⁻¹(x) + tan⁻¹(1/x). What is f′(2)?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Correct: d/dx tan⁻¹(1/x) = [1/(1 + 1/x²)]·(−1/x²) = −1/(x² + 1), which cancels 1/(1 + x²), so f′(x) = 0 (f is constant, π/2, for x > 0).

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This loses the minus sign from the chain factor −1/x² when differentiating tan⁻¹(1/x), so the two terms 1/5 and 1/5 are added.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This omits the chain factor −1/x² on the second term, giving 1/(1 + 1/4) = 4/5 for it, and then 1/5 + 4/5 = 1.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This differentiates only the first term and treats tan⁻¹(1/x) as if it were constant.

title: differentiate sums of inverse trigonometric functions whose chain factors cancel or add. (variant 1)
stem: For x > 0, let g(x) = tan⁻¹(x) − tan⁻¹(1/x). What is g′(2)?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This assumes the expression is the constant identity tan⁻¹(x) + tan⁻¹(1/x), but the minus sign makes the two derivative terms add rather than cancel.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This omits the chain factor −1/x² on the second term, giving 1/5 − 4/5 instead of 1/5 + 1/5.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This keeps only the derivative of tan⁻¹(x) and drops the derivative of the second term entirely.

title: differentiate sums of inverse trigonometric functions whose chain factors cancel or add. (variant 2)
stem: Let f(x) = 3sin⁻¹(x) + 3cos⁻¹(x) + x² for −1 < x < 1. What is f′(1/2)?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This uses +1/√(1 − x²) for the derivative of cos⁻¹(x), so the two inverse trigonometric terms add instead of cancelling.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This keeps the derivative of 3sin⁻¹(x) and drops the derivative of 3cos⁻¹(x), so no cancellation occurs.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This correctly cancels the two inverse trigonometric derivatives but drops the derivative 2x of x², which equals 1 at x = 1/2.

title: differentiate sums of inverse trigonometric functions whose chain factors cancel or add. (variant 3)
stem: For x > 0, let f(x) = tan⁻¹(2x) + tan⁻¹(1/(2x)). What is f′(1)?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This takes the derivative of tan⁻¹(1/(2x)) with the wrong sign, so its term 2/5 is added to 2/5 instead of cancelling it.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This differentiates only tan⁻¹(2x), whose derivative at 1 is 2/5, and ignores the second term.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This applies the arctangent rule without the chain factors: 1/(1 + 4) + 1/(1 + 1/4) = 1/5 + 4/5.

title: apply an inverse trigonometric derivative to an unspecified inner function given only values of g and g′.
stem: The differentiable function g satisfies g(2) = 3 and g′(2) = 10. Let h(x) = sin⁻¹(g(x)/5). What is h′(2)?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This forgets that the inner function is g(x)/5, so the factor 1/5 is missing from the chain-rule derivative of the argument.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This uses the derivative of cos⁻¹, which carries a minus sign, instead of the derivative of sin⁻¹.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This leaves out the square root: the sin⁻¹ derivative is 1/√(1 − u²), not 1/(1 − u²).

title: apply an inverse trigonometric derivative to an unspecified inner function given only values of g and g′. (variant 1)
stem: The differentiable function g satisfies g(1) = 4 and g′(1) = −3. Let h(x) = tan⁻¹(g(x)/2). What is h′(1)?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This omits the factor 1/2 from the derivative of g(x)/2, so g′(1) is used in place of g′(1)/2.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This puts g(1) = 4 instead of g(1)/2 = 2 into the denominator 1 + u², so the arctangent rule is evaluated at the wrong argument.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This uses 1/√(1 + u²) instead of 1/(1 + u²); the arctangent derivative has no square root.

title: apply an inverse trigonometric derivative to an unspecified inner function given only values of g and g′. (variant 2)
stem: The differentiable function g satisfies g(3) = 2 and g′(3) = 6. Let h(x) = cos⁻¹(g(x)/4). What is h′(3)?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This drops the minus sign from the derivative of cos⁻¹, which is −1/√(1 − u²).

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This omits the factor 1/4 from the derivative of g(x)/4, so g′(3) = 6 is used unscaled.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This leaves out the square root and uses −u′/(1 − u²) instead of −u′/√(1 − u²).

title: apply an inverse trigonometric derivative to an unspecified inner function given only values of g and g′. (variant 3)
stem: The differentiable function g satisfies g(1) = 3/4 and g′(1) = −2. Let h(x) = sin⁻¹(1 − g(x)). What is h′(1)?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This forgets that the derivative of 1 − g(x) is −g′(x), so the minus sign from the inner function is lost.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This leaves out the square root, using 1/(1 − u²) in place of 1/√(1 − u²).

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This evaluates the square root at g(1) = 3/4 instead of at the argument 1 − g(1) = 1/4.

title: diagnose the first incorrect step in a worked derivative that mixes product, quotient and chain rules.
stem:
A student differentiates h(x) = x²·sin(x³) as follows.
Step 1: By the product rule, h′(x) = (x²)′·sin(x³) + x²·(sin(x³))′.
Step 2: (x²)′ = 2x.
Step 3: (sin(x³))′ = cos(x³).
Step 4: Therefore h′(x) = 2x·sin(x³) + x²·cos(x³).
Which statement identifies the first incorrect step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Step 1 is incorrect: the product rule requires multiplying the derivatives of the two factors.
choices.rationale: The product rule adds two terms, each differentiating one factor, so Step 1 is correct as written.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Step 3 is incorrect: the chain rule requires the factor 3x², so (sin(x³))′ = 3x²cos(x³).
choices.rationale: Correct: The derivative of sin(x³) is cos(x³)·3x², so Step 3 is the first wrong step; the correct result is h′(x) = 2x sin(x³) + 3x⁴cos(x³).

choices.label: C
choices.text: Step 2 is incorrect: the derivative of x² is x.
choices.rationale: The power rule gives (x²)′ = 2x, so Step 2 is correct.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Step 4 is incorrect: the two terms of the product rule should be multiplied, not added.
choices.rationale: Step 4 correctly adds the two product-rule terms from Steps 1 to 3; its only flaw is inherited from Step 3.

title: diagnose the first incorrect step in a worked derivative that mixes product, quotient and chain rules. (variant 1)
stem:
A student differentiates g(x) = e²ˣ/(x² + 1) as follows.
Step 1: By the quotient rule, g′(x) = [(x² + 1)·(e²ˣ)′ − e²ˣ·(x² + 1)′]/(x² + 1).
Step 2: (e²ˣ)′ = 2e²ˣ.
Step 3: (x² + 1)′ = 2x.
Step 4: Therefore g′(x) = [2e²ˣ(x² + 1) − 2x·e²ˣ]/(x² + 1).
Which statement identifies the first incorrect step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Step 2 is incorrect: the derivative of e²ˣ is e²ˣ.
choices.rationale: The chain rule gives (e²ˣ)′ = 2e²ˣ, so Step 2 is correct.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Step 1 is incorrect: the denominator of the quotient rule must be (x² + 1)².
choices.rationale: Correct: The quotient rule divides by the square of the denominator, so Step 1 is wrong; the correct result is g′(x) = e²ˣ(2x² − 2x + 2)/(x² + 1)².

choices.label: C
choices.text: Step 3 is incorrect: the derivative of x² + 1 is x².
choices.rationale: The derivative of x² + 1 is 2x, so Step 3 is correct.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Step 4 is incorrect: the numerator should add the two products rather than subtract them.
choices.rationale: The quotient rule subtracts in the numerator, and Step 4 follows that pattern correctly from Steps 1 to 3.

title: diagnose the first incorrect step in a worked derivative that mixes product, quotient and chain rules. (variant 2)
stem:
A student differentiates p(x) = x³(2x − 5)⁴ as follows.
Step 1: By the product rule, p′(x) = (x³)′·(2x − 5)⁴ + x³·((2x − 5)⁴)′.
Step 2: ((2x − 5)⁴)′ = 4(2x − 5)³.
Step 3: (x³)′ = 3x².
Step 4: Therefore p′(x) = 3x²(2x − 5)⁴ + 4x³(2x − 5)³.
Which statement identifies the first incorrect step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Step 1 is incorrect: the product rule should multiply (x³)′ by ((2x − 5)⁴)′.
choices.rationale: The product rule adds two terms; it never multiplies the two derivatives, so Step 1 is correct.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Step 3 is incorrect: the derivative of x³ is 3x.
choices.rationale: The power rule gives (x³)′ = 3x², so Step 3 is correct.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Step 2 is incorrect: the chain rule requires the factor 2, so ((2x − 5)⁴)′ = 8(2x − 5)³.
choices.rationale: Correct: The derivative of (2x − 5)⁴ is 4(2x − 5)³·2 = 8(2x − 5)³, so Step 2 is the first wrong step.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Step 4 is incorrect: the exponent 3 in the second term should be 4.
choices.rationale: Step 4 only combines the earlier steps; the exponent 3 in the second term is correct, and the flaw lies earlier in Step 2.

title: diagnose the first incorrect step in a worked derivative that mixes product, quotient and chain rules. (variant 3)
stem:
A student differentiates q(x) = x·cos(x²) as follows.
Step 1: By the product rule, q′(x) = (x)′·cos(x²) + x·(cos(x²))′.
Step 2: (x)′ = 1.
Step 3: (cos(x²))′ = −sin(x²)·2x.
Step 4: Therefore q′(x) = cos(x²) − 2x·sin(x²).
Which statement identifies the first incorrect step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Step 3 is incorrect: the derivative of cos(x²) is +sin(x²)·2x.
choices.rationale: The derivative of cos u is −sin u, so Step 3 correctly includes the minus sign and the factor 2x.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Step 1 is incorrect: the product rule should differentiate only the second factor.
choices.rationale: The product rule differentiates each factor in turn, so Step 1 is correct as written.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Step 2 is incorrect: the derivative of x is x.
choices.rationale: The derivative of x is 1, so Step 2 is correct.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Step 4 is incorrect: the second term must also be multiplied by the factor x, giving −2x²sin(x²).
choices.rationale: Correct: Steps 1 to 3 are right, but x·(−2x sin(x²)) = −2x² sin(x²), so Step 4 drops a factor of x; q′(x) = cos(x²) − 2x² sin(x²).

title: combine product, quotient and chain rules with tabulated values of unspecified functions, evaluating each derivative at
stem:
The differentiable functions f and g have the values below.
x | f(x) | f′(x) | g(x) | g′(x)
1 | 3 | −2 | 4 | 5
4 | −1 | 2 | 6 | 3
Let h(x) = x²·f(g(x)). What is h′(1)?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This drops the product-rule term 2x·f(g(x)) and keeps only x²·f′(g(x))·g′(x).

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This evaluates f′ at x = 1 instead of at g(1) = 4, so the outer derivative is taken at the wrong input.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This omits the inner derivative g′(1) in the chain rule for f(g(x)).

Let h(x) = x³·g(f(x)). What is h′(1)?

choices.label: B

choices.label: D

title: combine product, quotient and chain rules with tabulated values of unspecified functions, evaluating each derivative at  (variant 2)
stem:

x | f(x) | f′(x)
2 | 6 | −1
4 | 5 | 3
Let h(x) = f(x²)/x. What is h′(2)?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This omits the inner derivative 2x when differentiating f(x²) in the numerator of the quotient rule.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This evaluates f and f′ at x = 2 instead of at x² = 4, so the table row used is wrong.

choices.label: D

title: combine product, quotient and chain rules with tabulated values of unspecified functions, evaluating each derivative at  (variant 3)
stem:
The differentiable functions f and g have the values below.
x | f(x) | f′(x) | g(x) | g′(x)
1 | 3 | 4 | −2 | 1
2 | 0 | 5 | 3 | −6
Let h(x) = f(x)·g(2x). What is h′(1)?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This omits the inner derivative 2 when differentiating g(2x), so g′(2) is not doubled.

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

title: find a second derivative of a composite or product of unspecified functions by applying the chain and product rules twic
stem: The functions f and g are twice differentiable, with g(1) = 2, g′(1) = 3, g″(1) = −4, f′(2) = 5 and f″(2) = −1. If h(x) = f(g(x)), what is h″(1)?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This forgets to square g′(1) in the term f″(g(x))·(g′(x))², using f″(2)·g′(1) = −3 instead of −9.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This drops the product-rule term f′(g(x))·g″(x), which contributes 5·(−4) = −20.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This multiplies the two second derivatives, f″(2)·g″(1), which is not what differentiating twice produces.

title: find a second derivative of a composite or product of unspecified functions by applying the chain and product rules twic (variant 1)
stem: The function f is twice differentiable, with f′(4) = 3 and f″(4) = −1/2. If h(x) = f(x²), what is h″(2)?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This drops the term 2f′(x²) that comes from differentiating the factor 2x, keeping only 4x²·f″(x²).

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This omits the inner derivative 2x when differentiating f′(x²), using 2f′(4) + 2x·f″(4) instead of 2f′(4) + 4x²·f″(4).

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This subtracts the product-rule term 2f′(x²) instead of adding it to 4x²·f″(x²).

title: find a second derivative of a composite or product of unspecified functions by applying the chain and product rules twic (variant 2)
stem: The function f is twice differentiable, with f(0) = 0, f′(0) = 2 and f″(0) = −3. If h(x) = e^(f(x)), what is h″(0)?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This keeps only e^f·f″ and drops the term e^f·(f′)² that arises from differentiating e^f a second time.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Correct: h′ = e^f·f′; h″ = e^f·(f′)² + e^f·f″ = e⁰(4 − 3) = 1.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This uses f″ + f′ in place of f″ + (f′)², forgetting to square f′(0).

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This keeps only the term e^f·(f′)² and drops e^f·f″.

title: find a second derivative of a composite or product of unspecified functions by applying the chain and product rules twic (variant 3)
stem: The functions f and g are twice differentiable, with f(1) = 2, f′(1) = 3, f″(1) = −1, g(1) = −2, g′(1) = 4 and g″(1) = 5. If h(x) = f(x)·g(x), what is h″(1)?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This omits the factor 2 on the middle term, using f′g′ instead of 2f′g′.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This keeps only f″g + f·g″ and drops the cross term 2f′g′.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This multiplies the two second derivatives, f″(1)·g″(1), which ignores the product rule.

title: find and interpret the second derivative of a function defined implicitly, substituting dy/dx before evaluating.
stem: The curve y² = 4x passes through the point (4, 4), and near that point y is a differentiable function of x. Which statement about d²y/dx² at (4, 4) is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: d²y/dx² = −1/8, so the curve is concave down at (4, 4).
choices.rationale: This differentiates 2/y as −2/y² and forgets the chain factor dy/dx = 1/2, which gives −1/8 instead of −2(1/2)/16 = −1/16.

choices.label: B
choices.text: d²y/dx² = 1/16, so the curve is concave up at (4, 4).
choices.rationale: This loses the minus sign when differentiating 2/y; the derivative of 1/y is −y′/y², which is negative here.

choices.label: C
choices.text: d²y/dx² = −1/16, so the curve is concave down at (4, 4).
choices.rationale: Correct: 2y·y′ = 4 gives y′ = 2/y. Then y″ = −2y′/y² = −4/y³. At (4, 4): y′ = 1/2 and y″ = −4/64 = −1/16 < 0.

choices.label: D
choices.text: d²y/dx² = 1/2, so the curve is concave up at (4, 4).
choices.rationale: This reports dy/dx = 2/y = 1/2, the first derivative, instead of differentiating a second time.

title: find and interpret the second derivative of a function defined implicitly, substituting dy/dx before evaluating. (variant 1)
stem: Near the point (2, 2) on the curve xy = 4, y is a differentiable function of x. Which statement about d²y/dx² at (2, 2) is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: d²y/dx² = −1, so the curve is concave down at (2, 2).
choices.rationale: This makes a sign error in the quotient step: y″ = −(x·y′ − y)/x² with y′ = −1 equals +1, not −1.

choices.label: B
choices.text: d²y/dx² = 1/2, so the curve is concave up at (2, 2).
choices.rationale: This drops the term x·y′ and uses only −(−y)/x² = y/x², ignoring that y′ is not zero.

choices.label: C
choices.text: d²y/dx² = 2, so the curve is concave up at (2, 2).
choices.rationale: This forgets to divide by x² and reports 2y/x instead of 2y/x².

choices.label: D
choices.text: d²y/dx² = 1, so the curve is concave up at (2, 2).
choices.rationale: Correct: Differentiating xy = 4 gives y + x·y′ = 0, so y′ = −y/x = −1. Then y″ = −(x·y′ − y)/x² = −(−2 − 2)/4 = 1 > 0.

title: find and interpret the second derivative of a function defined implicitly, substituting dy/dx before evaluating. (variant 2)
stem: Near the point (3, 4) on the circle x² + y² = 25, y is a differentiable function of x. Which statement about d²y/dx² at (3, 4) is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: d²y/dx² = −1/4, so the curve is concave down at (3, 4).
choices.rationale: This treats y′ as 0 when differentiating −x/y, so the term x·y′ in the quotient rule is lost.

choices.label: B
choices.text: d²y/dx² = −7/64, so the curve is concave down at (3, 4).
choices.rationale: This substitutes y′ = −x/y with the wrong sign, giving y − x²/y in the numerator instead of y + x²/y.

choices.label: C
choices.text: d²y/dx² = −25/16, so the curve is concave down at (3, 4).
choices.rationale: This divides by y² instead of y³; the simplified result is −25/y³.

choices.label: D
choices.text: d²y/dx² = −25/64, so the curve is concave down at (3, 4).

title: find and interpret the second derivative of a function defined implicitly, substituting dy/dx before evaluating. (variant 3)
stem: The curve x = y³ + 2y passes through the point (3, 1), and near that point y is a differentiable function of x. Which statement about d²y/dx² at (3, 1) is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: d²y/dx² = −6/125, so the curve is concave down at (3, 1).

choices.label: B
choices.text: d²y/dx² = 6/125, so the curve is concave up at (3, 1).
choices.rationale: This loses the minus sign: differentiating (3y² + 2)⁻¹ produces −(3y² + 2)⁻²·6y·y′, which is negative here.

choices.label: C
choices.text: d²y/dx² = −6/25, so the curve is concave down at (3, 1).
choices.rationale: This forgets one factor of dy/dx = 1/5 from the chain rule when differentiating 1/(3y² + 2).

choices.label: D
choices.text: d²y/dx² = −1/25, so the curve is concave down at (3, 1).
choices.rationale: This treats 3y² + 2 as if it were x, ignoring the chain factor 6y·(dy/dx) from the inner function.
